evidence_quotes.quote: This qualitative project utilizes semi-structured interviews, observations, shadowing, and analysis of primary and secondary documents to examine impacts and risk allocation of sustainability-oriented public–private partnership projects in Southern California.
Data analysis centered on identifying the distribution of risks between partners and the economic, environmental, and social impacts of seven infrastructure and three data-oriented PPPs.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 4, Section 3.2 Data collection and analysis
evidence_quotes.quote: Total interview time was 26 h and 42 min, with an average length of 65 min per interview. Respondents included staff from partnering organizations who were involved in partnership formation, design, implementation, operation and management, and/or project oversight.

Risk premiums, private returns of investment, the use of expensive technology of water treatment and provision, opposition to projects, and a shifting regulatory climate impacted the unit cost of water, which increased long-term costs borne by ratepayers.

Changes to water rates represent the changes to average water rates of Tier 2 water users. The changes to Rialto’s water rates include changes to both the water bill and the wastewater bill; changes to only potable water provision are between $25.38 and $42.98.

criterion_notes.c1: No. The paper evaluates project-level sustainability tradeoffs and partner risk allocation across 10 water-sector PPPs in Southern California (bulk seawater desalination, desert groundwater extraction, stormwater capture, recycled water for a recreational swimming lake, utility battery energy storage, three utility data-analytics collaborations, and one municipal water/wastewater system upgrade concession). It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (such as connections, disconnections, service exclusion, or household-level access barriers), touching ratepayers only indirectly via project-induced changes in average utility water bills (Table 6).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — the study examines institutional, contractual, and regulatory factors, specifically public-private partnership (PPP) contracts, inter-partner risk allocation, and multi-agency environmental permitting processes (CEQA, State Water Resources Control Board, Coastal Commission, Bureau of Land Management), with a brief secondary mention of a Proposition 218 rate protest in Rialto. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: No — the governance factor analyzed is PPP project delivery and inter-partner risk allocation for capital infrastructure and data-analytics projects (how public agencies and private firms allocate financing, design, permitting, construction, O&M, and wholesale demand risks, alongside project-management practices like partner communication, phased MOUs/off-ramps, and involving utility engineers in design), rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden on users, documentation/tenure requirements, disconnections/enforcement, or retail tariff/ownership rules directly governing access). Although private equity return premiums, wholesale take-or-pay agreements, and Rialto's concession debt-refinancing pass costs onto retail bills, the study does not examine retail tariff rules or regulatory structures directly governing household access.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Qualitative comparative case study of 10 Southern California PPPs using 27 semi-structured interviews with 21 respondents (from 7 public agencies, 3 NGOs, and 4 private companies), 4 non-participant observation windows, 4 facility shadowing tours, and primary/secondary document analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Yes (at the utility/average-bill level). Reports project-level changes in average Tier 2 customer water rates ($ and % changes in Table 6, relevant to affordability, including a 68%-115% combined water/wastewater bill increase in Rialto and $5/month or 6.25% in Carlsbad) as well as bulk local water supply capacity (acre-feet per year in Table 5), though compiled partly from secondary reports and without measuring household-level access, connections, disconnections, continuity, or household affordability burdens.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Identifies the cases and participant sample (10 PPP projects in Southern California and 21 organizational interviewees), exposure (PPP contractual risk allocation and facility permitting/project governance), project outputs/outcomes (partner risk distribution, bulk water supply in AFY, environmental impacts, and average customer water rate changes), and study design (qualitative comparative case study). Note that Table 2's body text on PDF Page 5 did not extract from the PDF graphic, but all 10 projects are identified in Tables 3, 5, and 6 and the main text.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in English.

study_design: Qualitative comparative case study (semi-structured interviews, non-participant observations, shadowing, and document analysis)
population_and_sample: 10 water-sector public-private partnership (PPP) projects in Southern California (7 infrastructure PPPs and 3 data-oriented PPPs); 27 semi-structured interviews with 21 staff respondents from 7 public agencies, 3 NGOs, and 4 private companies, plus 4 observation windows and 4 site shadowing tours
exposure: PPP project delivery and contractual risk allocation between public water agencies and private partners (allocation of financing, design, environmental permitting, construction, O&M, and wholesale demand/electricity-price risks, plus multi-agency environmental permitting regulations)
outcome: Distribution of project risks between partners, bulk local water supply additions (acre-feet per year), operational and environmental impacts, media/community contention, and changes in average Tier 2 customer water rates ($ and %)
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure), with c1 and c2 unmet under protocol scope. This qualitative comparative case study evaluates inter-partner risk allocation and project sustainability across 10 Southern California water-sector PPPs (seawater desalination, desert groundwater extraction, stormwater capture, swimming-lake recycled water, battery energy storage, three utility data-analytics projects, and one municipal water/wastewater upgrade concession). Although Table 6 reports secondary/project-level changes in average Tier 2 customer water rates, the study examines upstream PPP project delivery, procurement risk-sharing, and facility environmental permitting rather than household or community service access or any rule-type legal/administrative mechanism directly governing service access per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification.
